summary: MLD is used by an IPv6 router to learn which multicast addresses its neighbors want. MLDv2 adds source filtering, so a node can state interest in traffic only from specific sources, and it is designed to work alongside MLDv1. This internet-standard text obsoletes RFC 3810.

eli5.summary: It is the IPv6 version of telling the router which groups you want and which senders you want to hear. The router then sends only what you asked for.

subtitle: How IPv6 routers learn which multicast groups, and which senders, their neighbors want to hear.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 multicast router needs to know which multicast addresses have listeners on each attached link, and for source-specific multicast, which senders those listeners want or do not want.
tldr.mechanism: One router per link acts as Querier and sends General, Multicast Address Specific and Multicast Address and Source Specific Queries. Nodes answer with Reports that carry a filter-mode (INCLUDE or EXCLUDE) and a list of sources, and report changes right away.
tldr.outcome: Routers get per-link, per-source listening state to feed their multicast routing protocol. MLDv2 interoperates with MLDv1, and this Internet Standard obsoletes RFC 3810 and updates RFC 2710.

today: RFC 9777 is an Internet Standard published in March 2025. It obsoletes RFC 3810 and updates RFC 2710; it has not itself been obsoleted. Its changes from RFC 3810 are small: errata fixes and renaming the Reserved field to Flags so bits can be allocated through an IANA registry.

sections.title: What MLDv2 Does
sections.content:
Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) is used by IPv6 routers to discover multicast listeners, meaning nodes that want to receive multicast packets, on their directly attached links, and to learn which multicast addresses those nodes are interested in. A multicast router may itself be a listener, in which case it performs both the router part and the listener part of the protocol.

MLDv2 is described as a translation of IGMPv3 (RFC 9776) for IPv6 semantics. Compared with MLDv1 (RFC 2710) it adds source filtering: a node can report interest in packets sent to a multicast address only from specific sources, or from all sources except specific ones. That is what Source-Specific Multicast needs. MLDv2 is designed to interoperate with MLDv1.

MLD is asymmetric. Listeners and routers have separate behaviors, and the information gathered goes to whichever multicast routing protocol the router runs. A router only needs to know that at least one node on a link listens to a given address from a given source; it does not track each neighbor individually.
sections.eli5: Routers need to know who on the street wants which shows. MLDv2 lets each house also say which senders it likes or does not like.

sections.title: Listening State and Filter Modes
sections.content:
Upper-layer programs ask the IP layer to start or stop receiving a multicast address through a service interface, IPv6MulticastListen (socket, interface, IPv6 multicast-address, filter-mode, source-list). The filter-mode is INCLUDE (receive only from the listed sources) or EXCLUDE (receive from everyone except the listed sources). Each new request for the same socket, interface and address completely replaces the earlier one. MLDv1's Start Listening is equivalent to EXCLUDE with an empty list, and Stop Listening to INCLUDE with an empty list.

A node keeps state per socket and per interface. The per-interface state for an address is derived from all sockets. If every socket is INCLUDE, the interface record is INCLUDE with the union of the source lists. If any socket is EXCLUDE, the interface record is EXCLUDE with the intersection of the EXCLUDE lists, minus any source that appears in an INCLUDE record. An implementation MUST NOT use an EXCLUDE interface record when all sockets are in INCLUDE state.

Routers keep state per multicast address per attached link: a filter-mode, a Filter Timer and a source list with a timer per source. A router is in INCLUDE mode if all listeners are INCLUDE, and in EXCLUDE mode if at least one listener is EXCLUDE. In EXCLUDE mode the state is written EXCLUDE (X,Y), where X is the Requested List (no effect on forwarding) and Y is the Exclude List (blocked sources).
sections.eli5: Each house keeps a list: either "only these senders" or "everyone except these senders". The router then merges all the lists on the street into the smallest list that keeps everybody happy.

sections.title: Query and Report Messages
sections.content:
MLDv2 messages are a subset of ICMPv6 messages, identified by Next Header value 58. All MUST be sent with a link-local IPv6 source address, an IPv6 Hop Limit of 1 and an IPv6 Router Alert option in a Hop-by-Hop Options header. The Router Alert makes routers examine messages sent to multicast addresses they have no interest in. Reports may use the unspecified address if the interface has no valid link-local address yet. The checksum is the standard ICMPv6 checksum and MUST be verified on receipt.

The Multicast Listener Query is Type 130. Its Maximum Response Code gives the longest time a node may wait before answering; values below 32768 are milliseconds, larger values use a floating-point format. The S flag tells routers to suppress their normal timer updates, QRV carries the Querier's Robustness Variable (set to zero if it exceeds 7) and QQIC encodes the Querier's Query Interval. There are three variants: a General Query (address and source count both zero), a Multicast Address Specific Query and a Multicast Address and Source Specific Query. General Queries go to the all-nodes address ff02::1, and the other two go to the multicast address being queried.

The Version 2 Multicast Listener Report is Type 143, sent to ff02::16, the address of all MLDv2-capable routers. It holds one or more Multicast Address Records, each with a Record Type, a multicast address and a list of source addresses. If records do not fit in one message, they are spread over several Reports. MLDv2 defines no auxiliary data, so implementations MUST NOT send any and MUST ignore any they receive.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of notes. The router sends a question note, and houses send back an answer note listing their groups and which senders they want or block.

sections.title: How Listeners Behave
sections.content:
A listener acts on three events: a change of its per-interface state, a timer firing, or the arrival of a Query. Messages for the link-scope all-nodes address and for addresses with scope less than 2 are never sent.

When the state for an address changes, the node immediately sends a State-Change Report. Table 1 of the RFC gives the records: INCLUDE(A) to INCLUDE(B) sends ALLOW (B-A) and BLOCK (A-B); EXCLUDE(A) to EXCLUDE(B) sends ALLOW (A-B) and BLOCK (B-A); INCLUDE to EXCLUDE sends TO_EX; and EXCLUDE to INCLUDE sends TO_IN. To survive packet loss, the report is retransmitted [Robustness Variable] - 1 more times at random intervals in the range (0, [Unsolicited Report Interval]). Further changes in the meantime are merged into a new report.

On receiving a valid Query, the node does not answer at once. It picks a random delay up to the Maximum Response Delay and combines pending responses where it can. A General Query is answered with one Current-State Record per address it has state for, and implementations MUST NOT send a Report immediately on receiving a General Query, to avoid an ack-implosion. For a Multicast Address and Source Specific Query, the answer is IS_IN (A*B) if the interface is INCLUDE (A) and IS_IN (B-A) if it is EXCLUDE (A), where B is the queried source set. If the result has no sources, no response is sent.
sections.eli5: When you change your mind about a show, you tell the router straight away, and you say it a couple of times in case it was not listening. When the router asks a question, you wait a random moment before answering so everyone does not shout at once.

sections.title: How Routers Behave
sections.content:
On each link, one router is elected the Querier. All MLDv2 routers on the link hear the listeners and keep the same state so one can take over, but only the Querier sends Queries. The election uses the IPv6 address: a router that hears a Query from a lower address stops querying until the Other Querier Present timer expires. Since all queries use the fe80::/64 prefix, the comparison is on the last 64 bits. A router starting up assumes it is the Querier and sends several General Queries, spaced by the Startup Query Interval.

The Querier periodically sends General Queries to build and refresh state. When a State-Change Report says a node no longer wants an address or source, the Querier does not drop it at once. It lowers the relevant timer to the Last Listener Query Time and sends a Multicast Address Specific or Multicast Address and Source Specific Query, retransmitted [Last Listener Query Count] times. If no Report asks for it again before the timer expires, the address or source is pruned. This is the "fast leave".

Each source has a Source Timer, and the Filter Timer governs EXCLUDE mode. When the Filter Timer expires, the router switches to INCLUDE mode: sources in the Requested List move to the Include List and the Exclude List is deleted. MLDv2 only gives forwarding suggestions to the routing protocol and does not override multicast routing information. The S flag is set on repeat queries so that routers do not lower their timers a second time.
sections.eli5: One grown-up per street is the question-asker. If someone says they no longer want a show, the grown-up asks the street again a few times before switching it off, in case somebody else still wants it.

sections.title: Working with MLDv1
sections.content:
A Query's version is told by its length: 24 octets for MLDv1 and 28 octets or more for MLDv2. Anything else, such as 26 octets, MUST be silently ignored.

Hosts keep a Host Compatibility Mode per interface. Receiving an MLDv1 General Query sets it to MLDv1 and starts the Older-Version-Querier-Present timer; when that timer expires the host returns to MLDv2. Changing mode cancels all pending responses and retransmission timers.

Routers keep a compatibility mode per multicast address, set to MLDv1 when an MLDv1 Report (Type 131) arrives for it. In that mode the router treats an MLDv1 Report as IS_EX({}) and a Done as TO_IN({}), ignores BLOCK messages and ignores source lists in TO_EX. If an MLDv1 router is on the link, the Querier MUST use the lowest MLD version present, which must be configured by the administrator. Implementations are recommended to offer a setting that disables compatibility mode so that a network can run in SSM mode only.
sections.eli5: If an old-fashioned neighbor only speaks the old language, the newer devices switch to speaking the old language too until the old speaker goes quiet.

sections.title: Timers and Default Values
sections.content:
Most timers are configurable, but non-default settings MUST be consistent among all nodes on a link. The Robustness Variable tunes for expected packet loss: MLD is robust to [Robustness Variable] - 1 packet losses, the value MUST NOT be zero and SHOULD NOT be one, and the default is 2. Raising it on a lossy link also increases the leave latency.

The Query Interval defaults to 125 seconds; larger values mean fewer MLD messages. The Query Response Interval defaults to 10000 milliseconds (10 seconds) and must be less than the Query Interval. A larger value spreads Reports out and makes traffic less bursty.

Several values are derived. The Multicast Address Listening Interval MUST be ([Robustness Variable] times [Query Interval]) plus 2 times [Query Response Interval]. The Last Listener Query Interval defaults to 1000 milliseconds, the Last Listener Query Count defaults to the Robustness Variable, and the Unsolicited Report Interval defaults to 1 second.
sections.eli5: Timers decide how often the question-asker asks and how long everyone waits before giving up. The defaults are sensible, and every device on the street must use the same ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MLD has no cryptographic protection. Messages are not authenticated, their contents are not confidential and any message can be replayed. Replay can keep multicast state alive longer than group members need, which may lead to resource exhaustion in some devices. Anyone with access to the link can see which groups are requested, which is a privacy issue.

Nodes defend against forged off-link messages by checking that the source is a valid link-local address (or the unspecified address for Reports), that the Hop Limit is 1 and that the Router Alert option is present; otherwise the packet is dropped. On-link forgery is still possible. A forged Query from a lower address can steal the Querier role. A forged version 1 Query or Report can push listeners or routers into MLDv1 compatibility mode, and the RFC suggests a configuration option to ignore version 1 messages where source filtering is critical. Forged Multicast Address and Source Specific Queries could be used for denial of service, so a node stack could limit how many such queries or sources it records.
sections.eli5: The notes are not locked or signed, so someone on the same street could pretend to be the question-asker. Checks make sure the notes only come from the street itself.

fields.desc: Set to zero by the sender and ignored by receivers.

fields.desc: Standard ICMPv6 checksum over the whole message and a pseudo-header.

fields.desc: Zero on transmission, ignored on reception.

fields.name: Multicast Address
fields.desc: Zero in a General Query; otherwise the address being queried.

fields.desc: Bit allocations are described in RFC 9778.

fields.name: QRV
fields.desc: Querier's Robustness Variable; zero if it exceeds 7.

fields.desc: How many source addresses follow, 16 octets each.

fields.desc: Zero on transmission, ignored on reception.

fields.desc: Bit allocations are described in RFC 9778.
